paras: The attempted lynching of John Bowen took place early on June 15, 1888, at Union Bridge, Carroll County, Maryland, when a group of men took Bowen, a Black man accused of a razor attack on two Black residents, from the town lockup and tried to hang him. He escaped, was recaptured in Pennsylvania eight days later, and was convicted of assault with intent to kill in December. The first dispatch wrongly reported him lynched, and most papers described the would-be lynchers as Black men, which Bowen disputed.

According to the Westminster Democratic Advocate, on the night of June 13 Bowen met Otho Jones, a blind man, and Ida Milbury, both Black, walking home from Union Bridge. He was accused of slashing Milbury with a razor after she refused to go with him, breaking her jaw, and of cutting Jones nine times when he interfered. A Union Bridge dispatch gave jealousy as the motive, said Jones was not expected to live, and noted that Bowen had served a year in the penitentiary for an earlier assault on a woman.

Bowen was arrested on June 14 when he returned from Westminster on the 8:20 p.m. train. By his own account he had come back to arrange bail, and Constable Repp and a crowd arrested him with drawn pistols at Calvin Wentz's saloon. About one o'clock Friday morning a group broke into the lockup, carried him outside town, and put a noose around his neck at an oak.

Accounts of the escape differ. The Union Bridge wire said he was "strung up by the neck," motioned to speak, and slipped the slackened rope as the lynchers fired after him without effect. The Democratic Advocate said the rope proved too short and he leaped away while it was being lengthened. Bowen said his hands were left untied and "they never had me off my feet at all."

Rumors then had him secretly buried, armed in the woods, or hiding with relatives near Westminster, and Baltimore's Deutsche Correspondent wrote that only fear of another lynching kept him from surrendering. Deputy Sheriff Tyler followed him from Emmitsburg to near Greencastle, Pennsylvania, and took him on June 23 without resistance to the Westminster jail.

In a jail interview Bowen denied the assault and said the men were a large crowd of whites with two or three Black men, led by Ida Milbury's father, who carried the rope. He said he had given their names to his counsel, I. E. Pearson, but did not want them punished. No report of an arrest or indictment of any would-be lyncher appears in the coverage.
On December 4, 1888, a Westminster jury found Bowen guilty on both charges of assault with intent to kill Jones and Milberry; the report gives no sentence.

The first dispatch, headed "Colored Men Lynch a Colored Man" and "A Negro Lynched," said Bowen had been "hanged to an oak" by men "of Bowens' own race" and called it Carroll County's fourth lynching in two years. A same-day correction ran far more widely under headlines such as "Got Away from the Lynchers" and "He Fooled the Lynchers." The Emporia Weekly News added the subhead "A Masked Party Let a Coon Slip Through Their Fingers," and weekly digests carried the story into late June, some placing Union Bridge in Indiana.

The Democratic Advocate called Bowen "a Colored Desperado" and noted that Baltimore papers had "thoroughly advertised" Union Bridge over the affair, but it also reprinted the Sun interview, the only place Bowen's version appeared. The capture dispatch said he had been "terrorizing Carroll county," without naming a source, and the Waterbury Evening Democrat headed it "Will the Lynchers Try It Again." Reporting the verdict, the Sun's correspondent recalled the attempt as the result of "much indignation" over the assault.

The papers disagreed on who the lynchers were. The wire described twelve or fifteen masked Black men and the Catoctin Clarion "colored citizens," while Bowen said most were white and that some put handkerchiefs over their faces only later. Reports on the victims also shifted, from Jones "not expected to live" on June 15 to both recovered by late June.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Bowen
bases: A group took Bowen from the Union Bridge lockup at night, put a noose on him at a tree and fired at him when he ran, an attempted lynching that failed when he escaped (A2, A6, A37).

Twelve or more men seized Bowen from the lockup without authority to hang him for an alleged razor assault, but he escaped and was later recaptured, tried and convicted, so no one was killed (A2, A6, A37, A39).

The county-seat paper, the Union Bridge wire and Bowen's own interview agree that he was taken from the lockup, noosed at a tree and escaped (A2, A6, A37); the first wire's report that he was hanged (A1) is overturned by every later account and by his capture (A23, A37).

accounts.gist: A large crowd of whites with two or three Black men, led by Milbury with the rope, took him in a wagon to the tree; his hands were left untied and he slipped the noose before he was ever lifted. He denied the assault.

framing.detail: The first wire ran as 'Colored Men Lynch a Colored Man' and 'A Negro Lynched,' calling Bowen 'a bad character'.
The escape wire ran nationally under headlines such as 'Got Away from the Lynchers,' 'Lynchers Given the Slip' and 'He Fooled the Lynchers'.
The Emporia Weekly News headed the escape 'Judge Lynch Fooled. A Masked Party Let a Coon Slip Through Their Fingers'.
The Westminster Democratic Advocate called Bowen 'a Colored Desperado' but later printed his full account accusing a mostly white crowd.
The capture wire said Bowen had been 'terrorizing Carroll county'; the Waterbury Evening Democrat headed it 'Will the Lynchers Try It Again'.

conflicts.note: Every later report and his capture and trial show he escaped (A23, A39); the first wire was wrong.

record_check.dossier: One man, John Bowen (spelled Bowens and Bowans in early reports)
Masked colored men per the wires and Maryland papers; a crowd of whites with two or three Black men led by Milbury per Bowen
Seizure from the lockup, attempted hanging, pursuit and shooting; no killing
No one was killed; the only 'lynched' report (A1) was wrong

info: About 1 a.m., Friday, June 15, 1888 (A15 says Thursday evening)
Taken from the Union Bridge lockup to an oak about 200 yards outside town, in a field belonging to Granville Haines
John Bowen (also Bowens, Bowans), colored; not killed
Accused of assaulting with a razor Otho Jones, a blind man, and Ida Milbury (Mulberry, Milberry, Hollenberry), both colored, on the night of June 13 after she refused to go with him
Wire and Maryland papers: masked colored men; Bowen: a large crowd of whites with two or three Black men, led by Milbury, the girl's father
Lynching attempt failed; Bowen escaped, was recaptured, and convicted; no sentence reported
